claims.claim: Sending a webhook costs a few milliseconds of CPU, so the whole day is well under one core of real work.
claims.about: Ruby / Sidekiq sending outbound HTTP POSTs
claims.why: The benchmark measures servers receiving requests, not the CPU cost of a Ruby client making outbound HTTPS calls from Sidekiq.

claims.claim: Sidekiq threads are fine for this, because Ruby releases the GVL during network I/O.
claims.why: The only Ruby figure is ruby-rails in the I/O-wait test (279 req/s at 17% CPU), which reflects that server's thread setup, not Sidekiq thread concurrency during outbound I/O.

claims.claim: A Go service that sends in FIFO order with no per-customer isolation backs up the same way, only at a higher ceiling.
claims.measured: I/O wait: go-gin 20,235 and go-nethttp 18,905 req/s vs ruby-rails 279; plaintext: go-gin 53,941 vs ruby-rails 3,704
claims.why: Go measured far above Ruby in every test, so saying Go has a higher ceiling points the right way.

claims.claim: A fiber-based Ruby sender (Async/Falcon-style) handles thousands of concurrent sockets cheaply.
claims.why: No fiber-based Ruby server or client was benchmarked.

claims.claim: Ruby path: you may only buy 5–10x headroom.
claims.why: The measurements don't cover a tuned Sidekiq webhook sender against the current setup.
